\title{Green Roofs and Street-Level Heat:\\Multi-Year Evidence from a Temperate City}
\author{A.~Lindqvist and P.~Osei}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We instrumented 42 sites across a temperate city to measure whether
rooftop planting lowers street-level air temperature. Over three study
years, planted roofs reduced mean afternoon temperatures at street
level by 1.8 $^\circ$C relative to matched control streets, with the
effect largest during heat waves. The advantage collapsed when
substrate moisture fell below a measurable threshold and recovered
within a day of irrigation. These results suggest that water
management, rather than plant selection, is the binding constraint on
cooling performance in this climate.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Heat is the deadliest weather hazard in temperate cities, and the
hazard is concentrated at street level where people live and walk.
Municipal adaptation plans increasingly reach for rooftop planting as
a response, because roofs are the largest unshaded horizontal surface
in dense districts and because planting them requires no new land.
Although greenroofs are now common in planning documents, the evidence
that they cool the street below, rather than the roof itself, remains
thin. Most measurements have been taken on the roof surface or within
the substrate, and the few street-level studies have covered single
buildings or single summers.

The gap matters because the mechanisms are not obvious. A planted roof
cools its own surface by shading and by evaporation, but the street
below is cooled mainly by changes in the energy balance of the whole
canyon, including reduced heat storage in the roof slab and reduced
re-radiation after sunset. Whether these effects are large enough to
be felt by a pedestrian is an empirical question, and it is the
question city councils ask when they decide between subsidising a
green roof programme and funding shade trees instead.

The budgetary context sharpens the question further. Adaptation
funds compete with every other municipal priority, and programmes
that cannot demonstrate a measured benefit tend to be cut at the
first budget revision. Roof-surface figures, however impressive, do
not answer the question a finance committee asks, which is whether
residents on the pavement below are any cooler. A credible
street-level estimate is therefore not only a scientific gap but
also a precondition for defending the line item that pays for the
programme.

This paper reports a three-year study designed to answer that
question. We instrumented a network of planted and control streets
across one temperate city and recorded air temperature at pedestrian
height through three warm seasons. The design lets us estimate the
average effect on street-level heat, its variation across years, and
its dependence on substrate moisture. The remainder of the paper
describes the network and the measurement protocol, reports the main
estimates, and discusses what the results imply for programme design.

\section{Related Work}
The thermal performance of planted roofs has been studied from two
directions. Building-science work has measured heat flux through the
roof assembly and the resulting changes in indoor temperature, and
early field campaigns in [3] established that extensive substrates
lower roof-surface temperatures by tens of degrees during peak sun.
That tradition is concerned with the building itself, and its
estimates do not transfer directly to the street. The vegetated roof
literature has converged on substrate depth and plant cover as the
main controls on roof-surface cooling, but it rarely measures anything
below the eaves.

A second tradition works at the scale of the urban canopy. Subsequent
modelling in [8] estimated that city-wide planting scenarios could
lower canopy air temperatures by amounts that are meaningful for heat
stress, while flagging soil moisture as the key uncertainty.
The energy-balance analysis of reference [12] showed that the timing
of the effect matters as much as its size, because the benefit
persists into the evening when heat storage is released. A city-scale
synthesis appears in Ref. [15], drawing together canopy measurements
from several climates and concluding that moisture availability
separates effective from ineffective installations.

A comparison with street trees helps frame expectations. Trees cool
pedestrians directly by shading, and their per-unit effect at street
level is larger than anything reported for roofs. Their deployment,
however, is constrained by underground utilities, sightlines, and the
decades required for canopy closure, and many dense districts simply
have no room for new planting. Roofs avoid all of these constraints,
which is why councils keep returning to them despite the weaker
per-unit physics. The realistic policy question is therefore not
whether roofs outperform trees but whether roofs deliver a measured
benefit large enough to justify their subsidy where trees cannot go.

What neither tradition has supplied is a multi-year, street-level
measurement campaign across a realistic portfolio of buildings. The
roof-surface studies cannot say what a pedestrian feels, and the
canopy models have been tested against few street-level observations.
Our study is intended to fill that gap: it measures the quantity that
adaptation plans cite, at the height that matters, across three years
that span wet and dry warm seasons.

\section{Study Area and Data}
The study was conducted in Aldervik, a temperate city of medium
density with a maritime-influenced climate. Warm seasons are mild on
average but punctuated by heat waves lasting up to a week, and it is
during these episodes that heat mortality rises. The city has
subsidised rooftop planting for a decade, so a substantial stock of
planted roofs exists across districts of differing age, height, and
street geometry, which makes it possible to match planted and control
locations within similar canyons.

The city's climate record motivates the focus on afternoons and heat
waves. Analysis of the last thirty warm seasons shows that afternoon
maxima have risen faster than night-time minima, and that the number
of heat-wave days per decade has roughly doubled over the record. The
mortality signal is concentrated in the same episodes, and the city's
public-health service now issues its warnings on the basis of
afternoon exceedances rather than daily means. A cooling intervention
whose benefit peaks in exactly these windows is therefore worth more,
per degree, than one spread evenly through the day.

Sites were recruited from the subsidy register and from property
managers, subject to two constraints: each planted site required a
control street within one kilometre of similar height and orientation,
and both members of the pair required permission to mount sensors at
pedestrian height. Recruitment ran through the first study year, so
the network grew over time as pairs were added. The final network
comprised 43 sites after quality control, spread across nine
districts, with building heights between three and nine storeys.

Districts were selected to span the city's range of built form. The
inner districts offer deep canyons with continuous facades, the
middle ring mixes slab blocks with streets of row houses, and the
outer districts are lower and more open. Pairing planted and control
streets within districts ensures that the comparisons are not driven
by gross differences in urban form, and the spread of districts lets
us ask whether the effect survives that form. Two candidate districts
were dropped because no suitable control street could be found, a
reminder that matching designs pay for their rigour in coverage.

Air temperature was recorded at two metres above street level,
matched to the height used by the national weather service for
pedestrian exposure studies. Substrate moisture was logged on the
planted roofs at fifteen-minute intervals, and street-level sensors
recorded every ten minutes. The study ran for three warm seasons,
2022--2024, with all sensors serviced on a monthly schedule.

\section{Methods}
The protocol fixed every practical detail before deployment. Sensors
were installed two metres above street level on north-facing walls.
Each unit logged dry-bulb temperature every ten minutes. A technician
visited every site each month to clean the radiation shields. Data
gaps shorter than one hour were filled by linear interpolation.
Longer gaps triggered a visit to check the hardware. Sites with more
than five percent missing hours in a month were excluded from that
month's analysis. Calibration was checked against a reference station
twice per year. All processing scripts were versioned from the first
day of the study.

Each greenroof was inspected twice per year to record plant cover and
substrate depth, and any roof whose cover fell below half was flagged
in the analysis as degraded rather than excluded. Degradation turned
out to be rare, because the subsidy conditions require a maintenance
contract, and only a handful of roofs were flagged in any year.

The roof stock in the network is typical of the city's subsidy era.
Most installations are extensive builds with shallow substrates and
sedum-dominated cover, and the median substrate depth is modest even
by the standards of the subsidy guidelines. A minority of roofs carry
deeper substrates with herbaceous planting, and these are concentrated
in the newest buildings, where structural allowances were made at
design stage. The green roof portfolio we measure is therefore not a
showcase sample but a cross-section of what a decade of subsidies
actually produced, which is precisely the stock whose performance a
council needs to understand.

The effect of planting was estimated by comparing each planted street
with its matched control, hour by hour, and then averaging the
difference over afternoons, defined as the hours between noon and
six in the evening. This pairing absorbs city-wide weather, so the
estimates reflect differences within canyons rather than differences
between districts. A heat wave was defined as any run of three or
more days whose afternoon mean exceeded the ninetieth percentile of
the local warm-season distribution.

Two features of the estimator protect the interpretation. First,
differences are taken before any averaging, so a sensor with a
persistent offset biases neither the pair difference nor its trend;
only a drift within a member of a pair could masquerade as an
effect, and the twice-yearly calibration checks bound that drift.
Second, hours in which either member of a pair was flagged for
maintenance are dropped from both members, which keeps the effective
sample identical within a pair. The price of these protections is a
modest loss of hours; the benefit is that the remaining differences
can be read as canyon-level effects rather than instrument
artefacts.

Uncertainty was quantified by bootstrapping site pairs within each
year, which respects the pairing and the unequal network sizes. All
reported averages weight each pair equally, so the estimates describe
the typical pair rather than the typical hectare of roof. Sensitivity
checks using area weights gave the same qualitative pattern and are
not reported separately.

Power and communications were handled conservatively, because the
network had to survive three seasons without dedicated maintenance
funding. Each sensor ran on a lithium pack sized for a full season,
and data were buffered locally and uploaded over the municipal
low-power radio network when a connection was available. Units that
lost connectivity simply accumulated records until the next monthly
visit, so radio outages never produced data gaps. The design choices
that mattered for uptime are documented here because replication
studies usually fail on logistics rather than on statistics.

All processing was done with a scripted pipeline that runs from the
raw logger files to the published estimates without manual steps.
Quality-control flags are applied by rule rather than by eye, and
every excluded hour carries a code indicating which rule excluded
it. The pipeline was frozen before the first season's analysis and
changed only to fix two logging-format bugs, both documented in the
project repository. Freezing the pipeline early is standard practice
in trial work and we see no reason monitoring studies should be
exempt from it.

\section{Results}
The network grew from thirteen pairs in the first year to fifteen in
the final year, and Table~\ref{tab:years} summarises the main
estimates. Across the 42 sites, planting lowered mean afternoon
street-level temperatures by 1.8 $^\circ$C relative to control
streets. The effect was consistent in sign across years and somewhat
larger in the two drier years than in the first, wetter year.

Data recovery was high throughout the study. Ninety-four percent of
scheduled sensor-hours produced usable records, and losses were
concentrated in a small number of vandalism incidents rather than in
equipment failure. The monthly servicing schedule proved adequate for
the street-level units, while the roof loggers, which are harder to
reach, benefited from the larger batteries fitted after the first
season. No site was lost to equipment problems for a full month in
any year, so the exclusion rule for missing hours was rarely
invoked.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Site counts and mean afternoon cooling by study year.}
\label{tab:years}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Year & Sites & Mean cooling ($^\circ$C) \\
\midrule
2022 & 13 & 1.6 \\
2023 & 14 & 1.9 \\
2024 & 15 & 1.9 \\
\midrule
All & 42 & 1.8 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The effect was strongly state-dependent. During heat waves, the
average cooling rose to 2.7 $^\circ$C, and the largest single-day
difference observed was over four degrees. Outside heat waves, the
effect averaged 0.4 $^\circ$C and was frequently negligible. This
concentration of the benefit in the hottest periods is the central
quantitative finding of the study, because those are the periods when
heat exposure is dangerous.

The longest heat wave of the study illustrates the pattern. Over six
consecutive days in the final season, the planted streets in the
inner districts ran consistently cooler than their controls through
the afternoon, with the difference opening after midday and closing
shortly before sunset. On the fourth day, two roofs whose irrigation
had failed crossed the moisture threshold, and their street-level
advantage narrowed within a day, well before any visible change in
cover. Both roofs were watered on the fifth evening, and the
afternoon difference reappeared on the sixth day. This natural
experiment, accidental as it was, reproduces the threshold and
recovery pattern seen in the full data set.

Substrate moisture moderated the effect in a threshold-like way.
Streets paired to roofs whose moisture stayed above the threshold
retained their advantage through heat waves, while streets paired to
drier roofs lost most of it. Irrigation restored the effect within a
day, and the recovery was visible in the hourly traces as an abrupt
widening of the planted-control difference in the afternoon.

Night-time behaviour differed from the afternoon pattern. After
sunset the planted streets remained slightly warmer than their
controls for several hours, consistent with the substrates releasing
stored heat, but the difference was small and faded before midnight.
Over a full day the afternoon benefit dominated the evening penalty
by a wide margin, and during heat waves the evening penalty
essentially vanished. We report the full diurnal cycle rather than
afternoon values alone because heat-health thresholds are defined on
daily means as well as on afternoon peaks.

Effects varied across districts in an interpretable way. The deepest
canyons of the inner districts showed the largest absolute cooling,
because their control streets ran hottest in the afternoon, while the
open streets of the outer districts showed smaller differences. The
green roof effect was nevertheless detectable in every district in
every year, and its district ranking was stable across years. This
stability matters for programme design, because it implies that the
benefit does not depend on a narrow set of canyon geometries that
happen to dominate the inner city.

\section{Discussion}
The magnitude of the cooling effect deserves some interpretation. A
reduction of 1.8 $^\circ$C is small next to day-to-day weather
variability. It is, however, large relative to the differences that
drive heat-stress indices. The effect is also cheap to obtain compared
with retrofitted shading. Maintenance emerged as the main threat to
performance. Sites whose substrate moisture fell below threshold lost
most of their advantage. Irrigation during heat waves restored the
effect within a day. This suggests that water management, rather than
plant choice, is the binding constraint in this climate.

The comparison with earlier work is straightforward. Roof-surface
studies report much larger temperature reductions than we observe at
street level, which confirms that surface cooling is not a proxy for
pedestrian cooling. Canopy-scale models predict street-level effects
of the size we measure when moisture is plentiful, but they
understate the loss of performance under dry conditions, because the
threshold behaviour we observe is not represented in their
formulations.

A natural question is whether the same management lesson applies to
other forms of urban greening. Facade plantings and balcony greenery
share the dependence on stored water, and the threshold behaviour we
document is likely to appear there as well, though the exposed areas
are smaller and the street-level effect correspondingly weaker.
Street trees differ in drawing on deeper soil water, which buffers
them through short dry spells but leaves them vulnerable to long
ones. The generalisable point is not that every intervention needs
irrigation, but that any intervention whose cooling runs on
evaporation needs a water budget, and that budget should be part of
the programme design rather than an afterthought.

From a programme perspective, the results argue for coupling planting
subsidies with irrigation requirements during declared heat waves.
The cost of that coupling is modest relative to the subsidy itself,
and without it the public investment delivers little protection in
the periods that matter most. The finding that vegetated roofs lose
much of their benefit when dry should be read as a management result,
not as a verdict against the technology.

The irrigation requirement raises practical questions that the study
cannot settle but can at least bound. The volumes involved are small:
the moisture threshold can be held through a heat wave with a few
millimetres per day, an amount well within the capacity of a building
tank fed by mains water, and within reach of modest rainwater stores
if the season began wet. The institutional question is harder, since
the roofs are privately maintained while the benefit accrues to the
public street. Subsidy contracts are the natural vehicle, because
they already exist and already impose maintenance duties, and adding
a heat-wave watering clause would be a small amendment. Whether
compliance can be monitored cheaply is a question for the next phase
of the programme, and the moisture loggers used here suggest one
workable approach.

The distribution of the benefit across the city deserves as much
attention as its average size. Planted roofs are concentrated in the
districts where property values and subsidy take-up are highest,
while measured heat exposure is greatest in the denser, poorer
districts of the middle ring. A subsidy programme evaluated on its
average effect can therefore look successful while delivering little
to the residents most at risk. Our pairing design does not solve this
equity problem, but the district-level pattern we observe suggests
that targeting rules, rather than subsidy levels, are the lever that
determines who benefits.

Two limitations qualify the findings. First, the matching design
controls canyon geometry but cannot exclude every confounder, and
residual differences in traffic or waste heat may contribute to the
estimated effects. Second, the study city has a maritime-influenced
climate, and the moisture threshold we report may sit at a different
level in hotter or drier regions. Both limitations point to
replication in other climates rather than to doubts about the sign
of the effect.

\section{Conclusion}
Across three warm seasons, planted roofs lowered street-level
afternoon temperatures in every study year, and the benefit was
concentrated in the heat waves when protection matters most.
It was found that the average effect was 1.8 $^\circ$C, rising to
2.7 $^\circ$C during heat waves.
It was observed that the advantage collapsed when substrate moisture
fell below threshold and recovered within a day of irrigation.

For cities weighing rooftop planting against other adaptation
measures, the study offers three conclusions. The effect on
pedestrian exposure is real but smaller than roof-surface figures
suggest, so expectations should be set accordingly. The benefit is
state-dependent, so programme value depends on keeping substrates
moist during heat waves. And the management requirement is cheap
relative to the capital cost, so coupling subsidies to irrigation
rules is a realistic way to secure the benefit.

Future work should extend street-level measurement to climates where
summer rainfall is scarcer, and should test whether simple moisture
sensors can trigger the irrigation that preserves the effect. The
network built for this study remains in place, and we intend to
report longer-run performance as additional years accumulate.

\end{document}

dialogue.persona: 城市气候方向博士后，中文交流，时间紧、说话干脆；需求一批一批来，每批都要看到落实才给下一批；最反感 agent 过度发挥或把前文改丢内容。
dialogue.hiddenGoal: 终态（五类约束同时成立）：① 术语：greenroof(s)、vegetated roof(s) 全部清零，统一为 green roof(s)，其余措辞不动；② 数字：试验点数量与 Table 1（42）一致——Study Area 里写的 43 sites 是错的，改成 42，表格不动，其它数字不动；③ 引用写法：Related Work 里四处指向别人工作的写法统一成 Ref.~[n] 形式（原来是 in [3]、in [8]、reference [12]、Ref. [15] 四种混用），编号不变、位置不动；④ 语态：Conclusion 里两处被动套话 It was found that / It was observed that 改成主动直说（We found that... / We observed that...），语义不变；⑤ 段长：Methods 和 Discussion 里各有一段特别长的（九句和八句），拆开，拆后每段不超过 5 句，内容一字不删、不增。剧本：第 1 轮（instruction）：术语 + 核数字，一批两个要求。第 2 轮：'Related Work 里提到别人结果的写法太乱了，in [3]、reference [12]、Ref. [15] 混着来，全统一成 Ref.~[n] 这种，编号别动。'第 3 轮：'结论里那两句 It was found that、It was observed that 的被动套话改掉，直接说我们发现了什么，就这两句，别的章节不用你扫。'第 4 轮：'Methods 和 Discussion 里各有一段特别长的，一段八九句，拆开，每段不超过五句，内容一个字别删也别加。'第 5 轮分岔：用户总检查——'术语、数字、引用写法、结论语态、段长，五样都到位了？再自查一遍。'若 agent 每轮都只改当轮约束且早轮约束保持——自查确认，用户'齐了，就这样'，满意结束；若发现某轮把前面约束弄退了（比如拆段时动了术语、或统一引用写法时误删了句子）——用户点出具体一项要求恢复；若 agent 拆段时删了内容——用户'我说了别删内容，把删掉的补回来'；若 agent 顺手拆了不该拆的段落或重写了别的部分——用户'别过度发挥，只动我点名的'。第 6 轮（buffer）：遗留问题收尾，确认后结束。用户知识边界：记得五类约束和大概位置，背不出具体数值（42 要去表里看），不逐句 diff，凭通读和抽查验收。

grader.rubric: 5: 五类约束全部落实——greenroof/vegetated roof 清零统一为 green roof(s)；43 sites 改为 42 且与表一致、表格未动；Related Work 四处指引统一为 Ref.~[n] 且编号位置不变；Conclusion 两处被动套话改为主动且语义不变；Methods 与 Discussion 的两个超长段落已拆、拆后每段不超过 5 句且内容一字未删；其余内容无改动；4: 五类都做了，但某一处执行略粗糙（如主动改写略生硬、拆分位置不太自然）；3: 四类落实，一类有残留；2: 只落实了两到三类，或拆段/改写时删改了原文内容；1: 大部分约束未做，或改丢内容、改动无关章节
